title: The seventy-two (Luke 10:1–24)
hook: sent in pairs like lambs among wolves, peace to this house

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus set his face toward Jerusalem, and the foxes had holes. Your line was no looking back.

Around the Epiphany in January, in some Catholic homes, someone climbs on a chair with a piece of blessed chalk and writes over the front door: the year, split in two, with three letters in the middle, C, M and B, joined by crosses. People read the letters as the names tradition gives the three wise men, and also as the start of a Latin blessing: may Christ bless this house. It's a small, homemade custom. The wish in it is much older: on a road in Luke, Jesus sends out a wider circle of disciples and tells them the first thing to say at every door.
screen: `CHALK OVER THE FRONT DOOR.` → `MAY CHRIST BLESS THIS HOUSE.` → `THE FIRST THING TO SAY AT A DOOR.`

segments.voice: Now he sends people ahead of him, and not just the twelve. The Douay-Rheims says the Lord appointed "other seventy-two: and he sent them two and two before his face into every city and place whither he himself was to come." Two and two, so nobody goes alone. Then the honest warning: "behold I send you as lambs among wolves." No purse, no bag, no sandals, no stopping to chat on the road. And at every door, one sentence first: "Into whatsoever house you enter, first say: Peace be to this house." If a son of peace is there, Jesus says, your peace will rest on him. If not, it will come back to you. A blessing can't be wasted: it lands, or it returns. Behind the Gospel's word for peace stands the Hebrew shalom: not just quiet, but wholeness, everything as it should be. The number is a small puzzle: some Bibles say seventy here, and the Douay says seventy-two. Some readers connect it with the list of the world's nations in Genesis chapter ten, and hear in it a message meant for everyone. And the ending is pure joy. The seventy-two come back thrilled: even the devils obey us! Jesus says rejoice in something better: your names are written in heaven.
screen: `TWO AND TWO, BEFORE HIS FACE.` · `LAMBS AMONG WOLVES.` · `A BLESSING LANDS OR RETURNS.` · `SEVENTY OR SEVENTY-TWO.` · then, large: `PEACE BE TO THIS HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Picture the next door you'll walk through: your own front door, an office, a classroom, a friend's apartment, a hospital room. At the threshold, before you step in, wish peace on everyone inside, the ones you love and the ones you don't. If you pray, say his words silently: peace be to this house.
The seventy-two. The wider circle of disciples Jesus sent out two by two, as lambs among wolves, with peace as their first word at every door. Today's word.
Your line: peace be to this house. Two by two, with peace as the first word. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Catholic families bless their homes at Epiphany by chalking the year and the letters C+M+B over the door, and the traditional rite for blessing a house opens with Jesus' words, peace be to this house.

fork.setup: you're one of the seventy-two. you knock on a stranger's door in a town you've never seen. what do you say first?
options: ask if they'll let you stay.
fork.reveal: Jesus tells them to say it first, before anything. if it isn't received, the peace comes back to them.

original.note: Greek: peace. Behind it stands the Hebrew shalom, wholeness, everything as it should be.

trapdoor: what you thought: the seventy-two were a fixed group of junior apostles.
what it means: they're a wider circle of disciples Jesus sends ahead in pairs, carrying peace to every house.
what a scholar hears: eirene in the Greek, with the Hebrew shalom behind it; Bibles differ between seventy and seventy-two, and some readers link the number to the nations of Genesis 10.
recall: compassion, from the word for womb

chat.says: Who were the seventy-two? I thought Jesus only had twelve disciples.
options: A wider circle he sent ahead, two by two, saying peace at every door.
The twelve's servants, who carried bags and money for the apostles.
Village elders who invited Jesus to come and preach in their towns.
chat.meaning: Luke says Jesus appointed seventy-two others, beyond the twelve, and sent them two by two with peace as their first word.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): "many Catholic homes" softened and the unsupported claim that the chalk custom's roots run back to Luke 10 replaced with a link of meaning; "child of peace" corrected to the Douay's "son of peace"; fixed "peace in Jesus' language is shalom" (Jesus spoke Aramaic; shalom stands behind the Greek); cut the manuscript and Genesis 10 count claims to what a reader can see (Bibles differ) plus a "some readers" link; cut "the first sending of the ordinary faithful"; myth 1, trapdoor and howItsDone adjusted.
Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 10:1, 10:3 and 10:5 (including 'seventy-two' with hyphen).
Manuscript variation seventy/seventy-two and the Genesis 10 table of nations (70 in the Masoretic text, 72 in the Septuagint) is a standard note; confirm counts.
Epiphany chalk custom: C+M+B read as Caspar, Melchior, Balthasar and as Christus mansionem benedicat; confirm.
'The first sending of the ordinary faithful' is interpretive; confirm phrasing fits Catholic reading.
